A.explanation: Too small by about a factor of 7. It would need a period of about $7.7 \text{ ms}$, which is far longer than the 3.5 divisions seen on the trace.

B.explanation: One period is about 3.5 divisions at $300 \text{ } \mu\text{s div}^{-1}$, giving $T \approx 1050 \text{ } \mu\text{s}$ and $f = 1/T \approx 950 \text{ Hz}$.

C.explanation: Slightly too large. It corresponds to exactly 3.0 divisions per period, but the trace shows about 3.5 divisions from one peak to the next.

D.explanation: Much too large. It would need a period of only about $0.14 \text{ ms}$, less than half a division, and confuses the time-base scale.

hints: Look along the horizontal time axis and count how many divisions make one full cycle, for example from one peak to the next peak.

Multiply that number of divisions by the time-base of $300 \text{ } \mu\text{s div}^{-1}$ to get the period $T$, and ignore the $40 \text{ } \mu\text{V div}^{-1}$ y-gain because it controls amplitude only.
Use $f = 1/T$ with $T$ in seconds, remembering $1 \text{ } \mu\text{s} = 10^{-6} \text{ s}$, then compare with 950 Hz and 1100 Hz.
walkthrough: Count the horizontal length of one wave. From peak to peak on the screen is about 3.5 divisions.
The time-base tells the time for each horizontal division: $300 \text{ } \mu\text{s div}^{-1}$.
This is closest to $950 \text{ Hz}$. This is option B.
